titleStmt.title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities

dhq:abstract.p: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

The Siege of Orléans: Voices of Faith and Fire
div.p: The Siege of Orléans: Voices of Faith and Fire

The year was 1429. For months, the French city of Orléans had suffered under the iron grip of English and Burgundian forces. Smoke rose from the outskirts, the air heavy with despair and the scent of burnt grain. Soldiers starved behind the city’s walls, praying for a miracle.

Across the fields of Domrémy, a young peasant girl named Joan of Arc claimed she had heard divine voices — saints urging her to save France. “It is God’s will,” she told the skeptical nobles. “France shall rise again, and I shall lead her army to victory.” Moved by her conviction, Charles VII granted her armor, a sword, and command of four thousand men. Dressed in silver plate and carrying a white banner adorned with Jesus, the Virgin Mary, and two angels, she rode toward Orléans.
Among the troops marching behind her were Jacques, a thin but sharp-eyed archer trained with a crossbow, and Louis, his closest friend, a swordsman. “Do you truly believe she’s
been sent by God?” Louis asked as they crossed the Loire River.
Jacques adjusted his bowstring. “I don’t know,” he replied. “But if her courage is heaven-sent, that’s enough for me.”
When Joan entered Orléans on April 29, the city erupted in hope. Citizens leaned from windows, cheering. Soldiers who had nearly given up straightened their armor once more.
“Fear not!” Joan cried. “The Lord is with us. We shall drive them out before the week’s end!”

The following days brought fierce combat. The English garrisons, armed with longbows and cannons, rained fire upon the French positions. Joan rode through the smoke, rallying her men. “Do not retreat! The victory is near!” she shouted, lifting her banner high as arrows whistled past. Her voice, steady and sure, carried across the chaos.

At the Church of St. Loup, Jacques fired bolt after bolt into the enemy lines. Louis, sword in hand, charged through the breach beside Joan. “For France!” he cried, before being struck down in the melee. Joan knelt beside him briefly, whispering, “You have served God well.”

By May 7, the French launched a final assault on the bridge towers of Les Tourelles, the English stronghold over the Loire. Cannons thundered, fireboats set the river ablaze, and Joan, wounded by an arrow, still refused to fall back. “In God’s name, we must press on!” she commanded, her banner waving through the smoke.
By dawn, the English line broke. Trumpets sounded. The siege was over. On May 8, 1429, the battered French army stood victorious, and Orléans was free.
Jacques gazed at the sunrise over the Loire, the city safe once more. “She’s just a girl,” he murmured, “but she’s changed everything.”
News of the miracle spread across France. The victory at Orléans became a symbol of

divine favor and national pride, marking the turning point of the Hundred Years’ War. Joan of Arc’s faith had rekindled the spirit of a weary nation, and her name would forever stand among France’s greatest heroes and patron saints.
